title: Water sources, water quality and water demand
summary: Three things carry this subchapter: the demand figures and peak factors, the drinking water standards, and the population forecasting methods. The peak factors matter most in application — each component of a supply scheme is designed for a different demand, and using the wrong one is the standard error. Note Nepal's own standards (NDWQS 2062) and the specific problems of arsenic in the Terai and gravity-fed spring sources in the hills.

sections.heading: Sources of water
sections.body:
| Class | Sources | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **Surface** | River, stream, lake, reservoir, impounding reservoir | Large quantity, **variable quality**, usually turbid, needs full treatment |
| **Subsurface** | **Spring**, infiltration gallery, well, tubewell | Better quality, **naturally filtered**; may be hard or mineral-laden |
| **Rainwater** | Roof catchment, ponds | Soft and clean, but **intermittent** and needs storage |

**Selection criteria**, in the order they usually decide the matter: **adequate quantity** at the driest season, **acceptable quality**, **elevation** (gravity supply avoids all pumping cost), **distance** from the demand centre, **legal availability**, and **cost**.

**The Nepali context is distinctive** and questions increasingly reflect it:

| Region | Dominant source | Principal problem |
|---|---|---|
| **Hills and mountains** | **Gravity-fed springs and streams** | **Drying of springs**, contamination at source, landslide damage to pipelines |
| **Kathmandu Valley** | Springs, deep tubewells, Melamchi diversion | Over-abstraction, falling water table, contamination |
| **Terai** | **Shallow and deep tubewells** | **ARSENIC**, iron, and bacteriological contamination of shallow wells |

**Gravity-fed spring supply** is the mainstay of rural Nepal and deserves emphasis: it needs **no pumping, no power and minimal running cost**, which is exactly what makes a scheme sustainable in a remote community. Its vulnerability is at the **source**, so **source protection** — fencing, a properly built intake chamber, and control of sanitation and grazing upslope — is the critical measure and the cheapest.

**Arsenic in the Terai** is a genuine public health problem, not a textbook curiosity. It occurs naturally in the alluvial aquifer sediments, is odourless and tasteless, and causes **arsenicosis** with long exposure. Nepal's standard permits **0.05 mg/l** (the WHO guideline is 0.01 mg/l), and mitigation is by **testing and marking wells**, switching to a safe source, deeper or alternative wells, or **arsenic removal filters**.

**Intake works** must draw water **below the surface but above the bed**:

> **Below the surface** to avoid **floating debris, oil and surface contamination**
> **Above the bed** to avoid **silt and bed load**

Types: **river intake**, **reservoir intake** (often **multi-level**, so the operator can draw the best-quality layer as the level changes), **canal intake**, **lake intake**, and **spring intake chamber**. All are protected by a **trash rack** or coarse screen, and the approach velocity is kept low (around 0.1–0.3 m/s at the screen) so debris does not pin against the bars.

**Infiltration galleries** are worth knowing as the elegant intermediate option: a perforated pipe or porous conduit laid **in the permeable bed of a river** collects water that has already been **filtered through the bed material**, giving better quality than a direct river intake with no treatment plant. They are used widely along Nepal's rivers for small town supplies.

**Wells:**

| Type | Character |
|---|---|
| **Open (dug) well** | Large diameter, shallow; low yield; traditional |
| **Shallow tubewell** | Taps the **unconfined** aquifer; cheap, hand pump; **vulnerable to contamination** |
| **Deep tubewell** | Taps a **confined** aquifer below an impermeable layer; better quality, higher yield, needs power |

The shallow/deep distinction matters for quality: a **shallow** well draws water that has travelled only a short distance through the soil from a surface that may carry latrines, animals and waste, so **bacteriological contamination is common**. A **deep** well under a confining layer is far better protected.

sections.heading: Water quality and standards
sections.body:
**Quality is assessed under three heads**, and it is worth keeping them apart because the treatment each demands is different:

| Category | Parameters |
|---|---|
| **Physical** | **Turbidity**, colour, taste, odour, temperature, total solids |
| **Chemical** | **pH**, hardness, chlorides, sulphates, iron, manganese, **arsenic**, fluoride, nitrate, dissolved oxygen, alkalinity |
| **Bacteriological** | **Total coliform**, **E. coli / faecal coliform** |

**National Drinking Water Quality Standards, Nepal 2062 (2005)** — the figures to know:

| Parameter | NDWQS limit | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Turbidity** | **5 NTU** (up to 10 permitted) | Must be low **before** disinfection |
| **pH** | **6.5 – 8.5** | Below 6.5 corrosive; above 8.5 reduces chlorine efficiency |
| **Total coliform** | **0 per 100 ml** | **Non-negotiable** |
| **E. coli** | **0 per 100 ml** | Indicates **faecal** contamination |
| **Residual chlorine** | **0.1 – 0.2 mg/l** at the consumer | Evidence of continuing protection |
| **Arsenic** | **0.05 mg/l** | WHO guideline 0.01 |
| **Iron** | **0.3 mg/l** | Taste and staining |
| **Fluoride** | **0.5 – 1.5 mg/l** | **Both a minimum and a maximum** |
| **Total hardness** | **500 mg/l** as CaCO₃ | Aesthetic and economic |
| Nitrate | 50 mg/l | Causes methaemoglobinaemia in infants |
| Chloride | 250 mg/l | Taste |
| Total dissolved solids | 1000 mg/l | — |

**Fluoride is the interesting entry** because it has a **lower** limit as well as an upper one: too little causes dental caries, too much causes **dental and skeletal fluorosis**. It is the only parameter in the table where a deficiency is itself a problem.

**Why zero coliform is absolute.** Chemical parameters cause harm over years of exposure and are expressed as concentrations to be kept low. **Pathogens cause disease immediately**, and a single infective dose suffices — so there is no acceptable concentration. **E. coli** is used as the **indicator** organism rather than testing for each pathogen, because it is abundant in faeces, easy to detect, and its presence proves faecal contamination and therefore the possible presence of typhoid, cholera and dysentery organisms.

**Hardness** is caused chiefly by **calcium and magnesium** salts:

| Type | Cause | Removal |
|---|---|---|
| **Temporary (carbonate)** | Bicarbonates of Ca and Mg | **Boiling** — CO₂ is driven off and carbonate precipitates |
| **Permanent (non-carbonate)** | Sulphates and chlorides of Ca and Mg | **Lime-soda** process, or **ion exchange (zeolite)** |

Hardness is expressed as **mg/l of CaCO₃**. Classification: soft < 75, moderately hard 75–150, hard 150–300, very hard > 300 mg/l. Its effects: **soap wastage and scum**, **scale in pipes, boilers and geysers**, and higher fuel consumption. Very **soft** water, conversely, is **corrosive** — so neither extreme is desirable, and some water supplies are deliberately stabilised.

**Water-related diseases**, classified by transmission route — a standard question:

| Class | Mechanism | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Water-borne** | Pathogen **in** the water, ingested | **Cholera, typhoid, dysentery, hepatitis A, polio, diarrhoea** |
| **Water-washed** | Lack of water for **hygiene** | Trachoma, scabies, skin and eye infections |
| **Water-based** | Part of the pathogen's life cycle is in water | **Schistosomiasis**, guinea worm |
| **Water-related insect vector** | Insect breeds in or near water | **Malaria, dengue, filariasis, Japanese encephalitis** |

The classification is useful because it shows that **more water** solves the water-washed group while **cleaner water** solves the water-borne group — and the two call for different investment. In Nepal, diarrhoeal disease remains a leading cause of child mortality, and it is a water-borne and water-washed problem together.

sections.heading: Water demand
sections.body:
**Categories of demand:**

| Category | Typical share |
|---|---|
| **Domestic** | **50 – 60%** |
| Industrial | 20 – 25% |
| Commercial and institutional | 10 – 20% |
| Public (parks, street washing, fire) | 5 – 10% |
| **Losses and unaccounted-for water** | **15 – 20%** (often much higher in practice) |

**Unaccounted-for water** — leakage, illegal connections, meter error — is frequently **30–40%** in Nepali and Indian systems, and reducing it is usually the cheapest way to increase supply. A scheme that loses a third of its output has, in effect, paid for a third of its treatment plant for nothing.

**Per capita demand:**

| Standard | Figure |
|---|---|
| **Nepal — basic rural** | **45 lpcd** |
| **Nepal — urban piped supply** | **65 – 100 lpcd** |
| CPHEEO (India) — towns with full flushing | **135 lpcd** |
| CPHEEO — cities with sewerage | 150 – 200 lpcd |
| WHO minimum for survival | 15 – 20 lpcd |

The **domestic breakdown** under the 135 lpcd figure: drinking 5, cooking 5, bathing 55, washing clothes 20, washing utensils 10, flushing 30, house cleaning 10 — which shows immediately that **bathing and flushing dominate**, and that drinking water is a tiny fraction of the volume though it sets the quality standard for all of it.

**Variation in demand, and the peak factors** — the most examined and most misapplied item in the subchapter:

> **Maximum daily demand = 1.8 × average daily demand**
> **Maximum hourly demand = 1.5 × maximum daily = 2.7 × average**

**Each component is designed for a different demand**, and this table is the substance:

| Component | Designed for | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Source and intake** | **Maximum daily** | It must be able to supply the worst day |
| **Treatment plant** | **Maximum daily** | Same |
| **Pumps and rising main** | Maximum daily (allowing for the hours of pumping) | — |
| **Service reservoir** | Balances **maximum daily against maximum hourly** | Its whole purpose |
| **Distribution mains** | **Maximum HOURLY** | It must deliver the peak instantaneous demand |
| Service connections | Peak instantaneous | — |

**Using the wrong factor for the wrong component is the classic error.** Designing the distribution main for maximum *daily* demand gives inadequate pressure at the morning peak; designing the treatment plant for maximum *hourly* demand builds a plant 50% larger than necessary, since the reservoir absorbs the hourly variation.

**Why the reservoir makes this possible:** treatment and pumping run at a nearly **constant** rate over the day, while consumption **varies hourly**. The reservoir stores the surplus in the small hours and releases it at the morning and evening peaks — so the plant sees only the daily average of a peak day, not the peak hour.

**Fire demand** is short in duration but very high in rate, so it sizes the **distribution main and the reservoir reserve**, never the source. **Kuichling's formula:**

> **Q = 3182 √P** litres per minute, with **P** the population in **thousands**

Other formulae: **Freeman**, **Buston**, and the **National Board of Fire Underwriters**.

**Factors affecting per capita demand:** **size and character of the city**, **climate** (hot and dry increases it), **standard of living**, **type of supply** (metered supplies use markedly less than unmetered), **quality and pressure** of supply, **cost of water**, **sewerage** (a sewered town uses much more, because of flushing), and the extent of **industry**.

**Metering deserves note** because its effect is large and reliable: introducing meters typically reduces consumption by **20–30%**, simply because waste becomes visible and chargeable. It is the cheapest demand-management measure available.

sections.heading: Population forecasting
sections.body:
A water supply scheme is designed for a **design period** — typically **15 to 30 years**, and up to 50 for major works such as dams and trunk mains — so the population at the end of that period must be estimated.

**The design period is itself a trade-off:**

| Longer design period | Shorter design period |
|---|---|
| Fewer disruptive extensions | Lower initial cost |
| Economy of scale in construction | Capital not idle |
| — | **Forecast is more reliable** |
| Capital tied up in unused capacity | Frequent extensions, each disruptive |

So **components that are cheap to duplicate later** (pumps, filter units, treatment modules) take a **short** design period, while those that are **expensive or impossible to extend** (dams, tunnels, trunk mains, reservoirs) take a **long** one. That is why a treatment plant is built in stages on land reserved for the full ultimate capacity.

**The forecasting methods**, and the choice reveals an assumption about how the town is growing:

| Method | Assumes | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **Arithmetic increase** | **Constant** increment per decade | **Large, old, saturated** cities |
| **Geometric increase** | **Constant percentage** growth | **Young, rapidly growing** towns — but **over-predicts** for old ones |
| **Incremental increase** | The increment itself changes by a constant amount | A compromise; generally the most reasonable of the three |
| **Decreasing rate of growth** | Growth rate falls as the town matures | Towns approaching saturation |
| **Graphical extension** | The past curve continues | Quick, but subjective |
| **Comparative graphical** | The town follows the path of similar larger cities | Where analogues exist |
| **Logistic (S-curve)** | Growth is slow, then rapid, then slows toward a **saturation** population | **The most realistic over a long horizon** |
| Zoning / master plan | Growth follows planned land use and densities | Where a statutory plan exists |
| Ratio method | The town keeps a constant ratio to the region or nation | — |

**The arithmetic and geometric methods bracket the answer**, and this is worth knowing as a check: for a growing town, **arithmetic under-predicts** and **geometric over-predicts**, so the truth generally lies between them. The **incremental increase** method lies between by construction.

**The logistic method** is the most realistic because it recognises a **saturation population** — a town cannot grow indefinitely, being limited by land, water and employment. Its S-shaped curve captures slow early growth, rapid middle growth, and a levelling off. The difficulty is estimating the saturation value, which is why it is used for long horizons where the shape matters more than the precise figure.

**Where forecasting fails, and why the engineer should say so.** Population growth is driven by **migration** far more than by natural increase in most Nepali towns, and migration responds to events no formula anticipates — a new road, a political change, an earthquake, or the growth of a nearby city. Kathmandu Valley's growth over recent decades outran every projection made for it.

The professional responses are: use **more than one method** and present the range; adopt **staged construction** so capacity can be added when the demand materialises; **reserve land** for the ultimate capacity at the outset (the single most valuable and cheapest provision); and state the **assumptions and their sensitivity** rather than presenting a single number as fact.

In Nepal, the **Central Bureau of Statistics** census — conducted decennially, most recently in 2078 (2021) — is the base data, and the **Water Supply and Sanitation Divisional Offices** and the **Department of Water Supply and Sewerage Management** are the agencies that apply these methods to scheme design.

formulas.label: Peak factors
formulas.expression: maximum daily = 1.8 × average ;   maximum hourly = 1.5 × maximum daily = 2.7 × average
formulas.note: Source and treatment for MAXIMUM DAILY; distribution mains for MAXIMUM HOURLY; reservoir balances the two.

formulas.label: Fire demand (Kuichling)
formulas.note: Short duration, very high rate — sizes the distribution main and reservoir reserve, not the source.

formulas.label: Arithmetic increase forecast
formulas.expression: P_n = P₀ + n·x̄     (x̄ = average increment per decade)
formulas.note: Suits large saturated cities; UNDER-predicts for a growing town.

formulas.label: Geometric increase forecast
formulas.note: Suits young rapidly growing towns; OVER-predicts for old ones. Brackets the truth with the arithmetic method.

formulas.label: Incremental increase forecast
formulas.expression: P_n = P₀ + n·x̄ + [n(n+1)/2]·ȳ     (ȳ = average incremental increase)
formulas.note: Lies between the arithmetic and geometric results by construction.

formulas.label: Logistic (S-curve) forecast
formulas.note: The most realistic over a long horizon, because it recognises a saturation population.

formulas.label: NDWQS key limits (Nepal 2062)
formulas.expression: turbidity 5 NTU ; pH 6.5–8.5 ; E. coli 0/100 ml ; residual chlorine 0.1–0.2 mg/l ; arsenic 0.05 mg/l
formulas.note: Fluoride has BOTH a minimum and a maximum (0.5–1.5 mg/l). Zero coliform is absolute.
